justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I interpreted as a current price near 1030, with the trajectory staying relatively flat across horizons. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing level, expecting minimal overnight or intraday drift and only minor mean-reverting fluctuations. For the one-week estimate, I nudged the forecast slightly higher to account for a small positive drift assumption, consistent with a low-volatility, range-bound environment. The one-month estimate continues that gentle upward slope, reflecting a baseline assumption of gradual appreciation without any strong directional catalyst — essentially extrapolating a modest trend while acknowledging the mean-reverting tendencies common in many financial or commodity markets.

The confidence interval widths widen predictably as the time horizon extends, which reflects the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty under standard diffusion assumptions. At one day, the 26-point spread is relatively tight because there is simply less time for the price to deviate meaningfully from current levels. By one week, the interval opens to 90 points, incorporating the accumulated variance from multiple daily moves and the possibility of a sentiment shift or data release. At one month, the 190-point range acknowledges that a full calendar month introduces macroeconomic reports, central bank decisions, geopolitical developments, and position-squaring flows that can compound in either direction.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include sudden liquidity shocks, a surprise policy announcement from a central bank or major government, or an unexpected geopolitical escalation. On the upside, a short-squeeze dynamic or a positive macro surprise could propel prices well above the upper bound. On the downside, a risk-off flight, margin call cascade, or disappointing fundamental data could send prices sharply below the lower bound, particularly at the one-month horizon where there is more time for such shocks to materialize and propagate.

It is also worth acknowledging model limitations. My intervals assume roughly log-normal price dynamics with relatively stable volatility, which historically underestimates tail risk. Real markets exhibit volatility clustering and fat tails, meaning extreme moves happen more frequently than a Gaussian model implies. If realized volatility spikes — as it can during earnings seasons, geopolitical crises, or liquidity crunches — then even the one-day interval could be breached more often than the stated 10% probability outside the range would suggest.
